Name: Intel (x86-64)
SDKs & notable repos: Intel oneAPI, ISPC, VTune, SDE; intrinsics guide
Downloadable / offline docs: The Software Developer's Manual (SDM) ships as a ~5000-page PDF set, plus the separate Optimization Reference Manual
Notes: The SDM is the single most important document in x86 work. Volume 2 (instruction set) is the part you'll actually live in. Site 403s to bots but loads in a browser.

Name: AMD (x86-64)
SDKs & notable repos: AOCC compiler, AOCL libraries, uProf profiler
Downloadable / offline docs: AMD64 Architecture Programmer's Manual, volumes 1-5, all free PDFs
Notes: Read alongside the Intel SDM — they disagree in instructive places, especially on memory ordering.

Name: Arm
SDKs & notable repos: Arm Compiler, Arm NN, CMSIS, Streamline
Downloadable / offline docs: Arm Architecture Reference Manual (the 'Arm ARM') free PDF; per-core Technical Reference Manuals
Notes: Note the split: the Architecture Reference Manual is the ISA; the TRM is one specific core's implementation. People conflate these constantly.

Name: RISC-V International
SDKs & notable repos: The whole ISA is developed in the open on GitHub — issues and PRs included
Downloadable / offline docs: Unprivileged and Privileged spec PDFs built from the repo per ratified release
Notes: The only major ISA whose specification you can read the git history of. Hugely valuable for understanding *why* a design is the way it is.

Name: IBM Power
Downloadable / offline docs: Power ISA specification PDF, openly licensed
Notes: Fully open ISA since 2019.

Name: SiFive
SDKs & notable repos: Freedom E SDK, core generators, SiFive Insight
Notes: Commercial RISC-V implementer; manuals are a good bridge from spec to silicon.

Name: NVIDIA GPU architecture
SDKs & notable repos: CUDA Toolkit, Nsight Compute/Systems, CUTLASS, cuBLAS
Downloadable / offline docs: CUDA C++ Programming Guide and the per-architecture whitepapers (Hopper, Blackwell) as PDFs
Notes: The CUDA Programming Guide's memory-hierarchy chapters are the best free GPU architecture text available.

Name: Apple Silicon
Notes: Sparse official microarchitectural detail; the community reverse-engineering (Asahi Linux, Dougall Johnson) fills most of the gap.

Name: Rocket Chip
SDKs & notable repos: In-order RISC-V core generator written in Chisel; the original Berkeley generator
Notes: Start here if you want to read a complete, synthesizable CPU.

Name: BOOM
SDKs & notable repos: Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine — a superscalar OoO RISC-V core you can actually read
Notes: The best available open implementation of out-of-order execution. Read it after you've read Rocket.

Name: Chipyard
SDKs & notable repos: Full agile SoC design framework: cores, accelerators, RTL sim, VLSI flow
Notes: The integration layer that makes the Berkeley ecosystem usable as one thing.

Name: CVA6 (OpenHW)
SDKs & notable repos: Application-class 64-bit RISC-V core in SystemVerilog, Linux-capable
Notes: SystemVerilog rather than Chisel — easier if you came from industry RTL.

Name: Ibex
Notes: A realistic small core with a serious verification story attached.

Name: VexRiscv
SDKs & notable repos: Highly configurable RISC-V core in SpinalHDL
Notes: Good demonstration of generator-based hardware design.

Name: PicoRV32
SDKs & notable repos: Tiny size-optimized RISC-V core, single Verilog file
Notes: ~3000 lines of Verilog. Readable in an afternoon — the best first CPU to study.

Name: OpenTitan
SDKs & notable repos: Open-source silicon root of trust; exemplary documentation and verification practice
Notes: Worth reading purely as an example of how hardware projects *should* be documented.

Name: gem5
SDKs & notable repos: The standard architecture research simulator: CPU models, cache hierarchies, full-system boot
Notes: If you read an architecture paper with simulated results, it was probably gem5.

Name: QEMU
SDKs & notable repos: Functional emulation and virtualization across every major ISA; TCG dynamic translation
Notes: Functional, not timing-accurate — know the difference before you cite numbers.

Name: Spike
SDKs & notable repos: The RISC-V golden reference ISA simulator
Notes: What 'correct' means for RISC-V in practice.

Name: Verilator
SDKs & notable repos: Compiles Verilog/SystemVerilog to fast C++ — the free path to cycle-accurate RTL simulation
Notes: Fast enough to boot Linux on an RTL model. Makes serious hardware work possible without licences.

Name: Ramulator 2
SDKs & notable repos: Cycle-accurate DRAM simulator covering modern standards
Notes: From Onur Mutlu's SAFARI group.

Name: DRAMsim3
SDKs & notable repos: Widely used DRAM timing and power model

Name: CACTI
Notes: The standard tool for 'how big and how slow would this cache be?'

Name: Gemmini
SDKs & notable repos: Systolic-array ML accelerator generator integrated with Chipyard
Notes: The accessible on-ramp to accelerator architecture.

Name: Chisel
SDKs & notable repos: Scala-embedded hardware construction language behind Rocket, BOOM and Chipyard
Notes: Generators rather than instances — a genuinely different way to think about RTL.

Name: Yosys
SDKs & notable repos: Open-source Verilog synthesis; the backbone of the open silicon toolchain

Name: OpenROAD
Notes: Tapeout-capable, entirely open.

Name: OpenLane
SDKs & notable repos: Automated RTL-to-GDSII flow wrapping OpenROAD + Yosys
Notes: The practical entry point to open silicon.

Name: SkyWater SKY130 PDK
SDKs & notable repos: The first fully open process design kit — real, fabricable silicon
Notes: Combined with OpenLane and Efabless shuttles, you can actually tape out a chip.

Name: Agner Fog's optimization manuals
SDKs & notable repos: Instruction tables, microarchitecture guide, calling conventions, vector class library
Downloadable / offline docs: Five free PDFs, continuously updated since the 1990s
Notes: The instruction tables and the microarchitecture manual are indispensable and have no official equivalent.

Name: uops.info
SDKs & notable repos: Automatically measured latency, throughput and port usage for x86 instructions
Notes: Where you go when the vendor manual is vague or wrong about instruction cost.

Name: llvm-mca
SDKs & notable repos: Static machine-code analyzer that predicts throughput from LLVM's scheduling models
Notes: Fast way to reason about a hot loop without running it.

Name: Perf Ninja
SDKs & notable repos: Self-paced performance-optimization exercises with automated verification
Notes: Pairs with the free book 'Performance Analysis and Tuning on Modern CPUs'.

Name: Algorithmica HPC
SDKs & notable repos: Free online book on modern hardware performance: caches, SIMD, branch prediction, pipelining
Notes: Exceptionally good and far too little known.

Name: Compiler Explorer (godbolt)
SDKs & notable repos: Compile any language with any compiler and see the assembly instantly; self-hostable
Downloadable / offline docs: Entire site runs locally from the repo
Notes: The fastest feedback loop that exists for understanding what the machine actually does. Use it constantly.

Name: Intel Intrinsics Guide
SDKs & notable repos: Searchable reference for every x86 SIMD intrinsic with latency and throughput
Downloadable / offline docs: Web application; data embedded in the page
Notes: 403s to bots, loads in a browser. Indispensable for SIMD work.

Name: Chips and Cheese
SDKs & notable repos: Independent microarchitecture analysis with original microbenchmarks
Notes: Currently the best independent source for measured details on new CPUs and GPUs that vendors do not publish.

Name: Real World Technologies
Notes: The archive of deep-dive articles on past architectures remains the best written material of its kind.

Name: OpenSBI
SDKs & notable repos: RISC-V Supervisor Binary Interface reference implementation
Notes: The firmware layer between your core and an operating system. Needed the moment you try to boot Linux on your own design.

Name: LiteX
SDKs & notable repos: Python-based SoC builder supporting dozens of FPGA boards and soft cores
Notes: The quickest practical route from an FPGA board to a working SoC running Linux.

Name: Amaranth HDL
Notes: A gentler entry into generator-based hardware design than Chisel if you already write Python.

Name: cocotb
SDKs & notable repos: Write RTL testbenches in Python against Verilator, Icarus or commercial simulators
Notes: Verification without learning SystemVerilog testbench constructs. Pairs well with Verilator.

Name: arXiv
SDKs & notable repos: Preprints across all of CS; most systems, ML and PL work appears here before publication
Downloadable / offline docs: Every paper is a free PDF. Bulk access documented at https://info.arxiv.org/help/bulk_data/index.html; a full-text API at export.arxiv.org
Notes: Not peer-reviewed. Treat an arXiv-only paper as a claim, not a result — but it is where you will read almost everything first.

Name: ar5iv
SDKs & notable repos: Renders any arXiv paper as responsive HTML instead of PDF
Notes: Makes papers readable on a phone and searchable in-page. Underused.

Name: alphaXiv
SDKs & notable repos: arXiv papers with a public comment and discussion layer
Notes: Useful when a paper is contested — the discussion often contains the critique you were looking for.

Name: Semantic Scholar
SDKs & notable repos: 200M+ papers with citation graph, influential-citation scoring and TLDR summaries
Downloadable / offline docs: Free Graph API (https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/api), bulk datasets available on request
Notes: The best free citation graph. 'Highly influential citations' is a genuinely useful filter for finding what actually mattered.

Name: OpenAlex
SDKs & notable repos: Fully open catalogue of works, authors, venues and institutions; successor to Microsoft Academic Graph
Downloadable / offline docs: Entirely free API with no key required; complete database snapshots downloadable
Notes: The only large-scale bibliographic database that is open all the way down, including bulk snapshots.

Name: DBLP
SDKs & notable repos: Authoritative CS bibliography — complete author and venue listings
Notes: The fastest way to find everything a given researcher has published, and to see a conference's full programme by year.

Name: OpenReview
SDKs & notable repos: ICLR, NeurIPS, COLM and dozens of other venues — papers plus the full review threads
Notes: Reading the reviews and author rebuttals teaches you how the field evaluates work. Nothing else exposes this.

Name: CORE
SDKs & notable repos: Aggregates 300M+ open-access papers from repositories worldwide
Notes: Good for finding the green open-access copy when a publisher's version is paywalled.

Name: Unpaywall
SDKs & notable repos: Finds legal free copies of paywalled papers via DOI
Notes: Legal, author-deposited copies only. Install the extension and most paywalls simply stop appearing.

Name: Papers We Love
SDKs & notable repos: A curated, categorised repository of classic CS papers with local meetup talks
Downloadable / offline docs: Repo cloneable; many PDFs mirrored in-repo
Notes: The best starting point if you do not yet know which papers matter in a subfield.

Name: The Morning Paper (archive)
Notes: No longer updated, but the back catalogue of ~1000 summarised papers is one of the great free CS resources.

Name: USENIX Proceedings
SDKs & notable repos: OSDI, SOSP (co-published), NSDI, ATC, FAST, Security — the core systems venues
Downloadable / offline docs: Every paper free, immediately, with no membership. Often with recorded talks
Notes: USENIX made everything open access years before the rest of the field. If a systems paper exists, check here first.

Name: ACM Digital Library
SDKs & notable repos: SIGMOD, ASPLOS, PLDI, POPL, SoCC and the ACM journals
Downloadable / offline docs: Partly open: ACM Open and author-paid OA papers are free; others are paywalled
Notes: 403s to automated clients; loads in a browser. For paywalled items, check arXiv, the author's homepage or Unpaywall first — the free copy usually exists.

Name: IEEE Xplore
SDKs & notable repos: ISCA, MICRO, HPCA and the IEEE journals
Notes: Almost always worth searching the author's page or arXiv instead. Architecture authors in particular post preprints widely.

Name: DROPS / LIPIcs (Dagstuhl)
SDKs & notable repos: ECOOP, ITP, CONCUR, SAT and many theory venues
Downloadable / offline docs: 100% open access, free PDFs, Creative Commons licensed
Notes: A fully open publisher. Every paper, always free, no exceptions.

Name: arXiv cs.AR (Hardware Architecture)
Notes: Lower volume than cs.LG; genuinely feasible to skim weekly.

Name: ACM SIGARCH
SDKs & notable repos: The architecture special interest group; runs 'Computer Architecture Today'
Downloadable / offline docs: Blog free; proceedings via ACM DL
Notes: The blog is the field's informal commentary channel — often where debates happen before they reach papers.

Name: Hot Chips
SDKs & notable repos: Industry symposium where vendors present real shipping silicon
Downloadable / offline docs: Slide decks and many talks posted free after each year
Notes: The only venue where you reliably get microarchitectural detail on products straight from the designers.

Name: NVIDIA Research
Notes: Read with the per-architecture whitepapers; the research papers explain the reasoning.

Name: Onur Mutlu's publications
Downloadable / offline docs: All papers free from the page
Notes: An entire subfield's output, all free, organised by topic, with matching lecture videos.

Name: Nand2Tetris
Notes: From NAND gates to an OS and a compiler, in twelve projects. Free, self-contained, and the single best first course in this field.

Name: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)
Notes: The textbook that connects C to the machine. Lab assignments (bomb lab, cache lab, attack lab) are public and excellent.

Name: CMU 15-213 Introduction to Computer Systems
Notes: The course CS:APP was written for. Slides and lab handouts public.

Name: MIT 6.004 Computation Structures
Notes: Full OCW materials from digital logic up to a working processor.

Name: Berkeley CS152 — Computer Architecture and Engineering
Notes: Undergraduate pipelining, caches, and out-of-order execution. Slides public per semester.

Name: Berkeley CS252 — Graduate Computer Architecture
Notes: The graduate follow-on, paper-driven.

Name: ETH Zürich Digital Design & Computer Architecture (Onur Mutlu)
Notes: Complete slide decks, labs and exams, all free.

Name: Onur Mutlu lecture videos
Notes: Years of full-length recorded architecture lectures. Probably the largest free architecture video archive anywhere.

Name: RISC-V unprivileged ISA spec
Notes: Start with RISC-V rather than x86. It is small, clean, and designed to be taught.

Name: RISC-V ISA manual source
Notes: Read the spec's git history when a design choice puzzles you.

Name: Intel SDM Volume 2 (instruction reference)
Notes: Reference, not reading. Learn to navigate it rather than to read it.

Name: Arm Architecture Reference Manual
Notes: Read the exception model and memory model chapters — those are where Arm differs most from x86.

Name: PicoRV32
Notes: Read a complete working CPU in one sitting, then modify it.

Name: Verilator
Notes: Simulate your RTL for free, fast enough to be interesting.

Name: Spike (RISC-V reference sim)
Notes: Compare your implementation against the golden model.

Name: QEMU
Notes: Understand emulation before you tackle timing simulation.

Name: learning gem5
Notes: Follow the 'Learning gem5' tutorial track before touching research configs.

Name: Papers We Love
Notes: Start here when you do not yet know which papers matter. Curated by subfield, with recorded talks.

Name: The Morning Paper archive
Notes: Around a thousand papers summarised in plain language. No longer updated; still one of the best free CS resources.

Name: Semantic Scholar
Notes: Free citation graph. The 'highly influential citations' filter is the fastest way to find what a paper actually changed.

Name: Unpaywall
Notes: Install the extension. Most paywalls stop appearing, legally, because the author deposited a copy.

Name: ar5iv
Notes: Read any arXiv paper as HTML instead of a two-column PDF. Swap arxiv.org/abs for ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html.

Name: BOOM out-of-order core
Notes: The clearest readable implementation of register renaming, issue queues and speculation.

Name: BOOM documentation
Notes: Explains the microarchitecture before you dive into the Chisel.

Name: Rocket Chip
Notes: The in-order counterpart. Diff the two to isolate what OoO actually costs.

Name: CVA6
Notes: Same class of core in SystemVerilog — useful if Chisel is the obstacle.

Name: Agner Fog microarchitecture manual
Notes: Per-generation detail on real Intel, AMD and VIA pipelines that vendors do not publish.

Name: uops.info
Notes: Measured ground truth for instruction cost.

Name: Ramulator 2
Notes: Model DRAM properly instead of assuming fixed latency.

Name: DRAMsim3
Notes: Alternative DRAM model; cross-check results across both.

Name: CACTI
Notes: Put area and energy numbers on your cache design choices.

Name: Linux kernel memory-management docs
Notes: Where the architecture meets the OS: TLBs, huge pages, NUMA.

Name: Chipyard
Notes: Integrate cores, accelerators and peripherals into a simulatable, synthesizable SoC.

Name: Chisel
Notes: The generator-based design approach the Berkeley stack is built on.

Name: Yosys
Notes: Open synthesis.

Name: OpenROAD
Notes: Open place and route, all the way to GDSII.

Name: OpenLane
Notes: The automated flow that ties it together.

Name: SkyWater SKY130 PDK
Notes: A real, open process. Your design can actually be fabricated.

Name: OpenTitan
Notes: Study this for verification methodology and documentation discipline, not just the design.

Name: Gemmini
Notes: Systolic-array generator — the accessible route into ML accelerator design.

Name: CUDA C++ Programming Guide
Notes: The memory hierarchy and warp-execution chapters are real architecture documentation.

Name: CUDA samples
Notes: Reference kernels showing what the hardware rewards.

Name: Triton
Notes: Where compiler design and GPU architecture meet; see the PL/compilers index too.

Name: Algorithmica HPC
Notes: Free book: SIMD, cache-aware algorithms, branch prediction, with measurements throughout.

Name: Perf Ninja
Notes: Graded optimization exercises against real hardware counters.

Name: easyperf
Notes: Companion blog and the free performance-tuning book.

Name: llvm-mca
Notes: Static throughput analysis of your hot loop.

Name: Linux perf
Notes: Counter-based measurement on real silicon.

Name: ISCA
Notes: The flagship architecture conference.

Name: MICRO
Notes: Microarchitecture-focused; often the most readable of the four.

Name: ASPLOS
Notes: Where architecture, OS and languages intersect — the most cross-cutting venue.

Name: HPCA
Notes: High-performance architecture.

Name: gem5
Notes: Learn it if you intend to publish; most results in these venues are produced with it.
